title: In those days (Luke 2:1–7)
hook: an emperor counts his people, and God arrives uncounted

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Benedictus: Zechariah's tongue loosed into a song of the dayspring. Your line was the dayspring from on high.

Somewhere in Rome, an order goes out: count everyone, so the empire knows who it can tax. It's the kind of thing powerful people do without thinking twice: a line in a decree, and ordinary lives rearranged. Families pack up and go, each to their own city, to be registered. Among them, walking from Nazareth in Galilee to Bethlehem in Judea, are Joseph, of the house of David, and Mary, the young woman he's engaged to, great with child. The emperor will never hear their names. He's counting heads, not looking at faces.

Luke opens the scene like a history book, in the King James Bible: "And it came to pass in those days, that there went out a decree from Caesar Augustus, that all the world should be taxed." Some readers puzzle over how this census fits other records of the time, and Luke doesn't stop to explain. He cares about the contrast. The emperor's decree moves Joseph and Mary to Bethlehem, David's town, little Bethlehem from Micah, without the emperor ever knowing. Then the birth, in two verses: "she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn." That's it. No angels yet, no star. A feeding trough for a crib. And notice what isn't there: no innkeeper. Nobody slams a door. Luke's Greek word for inn is the one he uses later for the guestchamber where Jesus eats the Passover with his friends. So some scholars picture a family house with its guest room already full, and the baby laid where the animals fed. The emperor sits at the center of the world, counting. In the Christian telling, God arrives at its edge, uncounted, in a crowded place, in a feeding trough. Some see a hint of the end of Luke's story, when his body is wrapped in linen and laid in a tomb hewn in stone.
screen: `THE CENTER COUNTS; GOD COMES TO THE EDGE.`
then, large: `THERE WAS NO ROOM FOR THEM IN THE INN.`

segments.voice: Think of the biggest story in today's news, big names, big numbers, and look underneath it for the people at its edges who'll never be named: a family packing up, a nurse on a night shift, a child somewhere in the crowd. Pick one and hold them in mind for a moment, by face, not by number. If you pray, pray for them; if not, simply let them matter to you for a minute.
Kataluma, Luke's Greek word for a guest room, usually translated inn: the opening of his birth story, where an emperor counts the world and Jesus is born at its edge, laid in a manger.
Your line: not counted, but there. Born at the edge, where the animals fed. See you tomorrow.

chat.says: Why does Luke start the Christmas story with a Roman emperor?
options: For contrast: an emperor counts the world; Jesus is born at its edge.
To show Augustus knew about the birth and sent gifts to Bethlehem.
To show the emperor ordered Joseph and Mary to Bethlehem by name.
chat.meaning: Augustus's decree moves Joseph and Mary to Bethlehem without the emperor ever knowing. In the Christian telling, God arrives at the edge, uncounted, in a manger.

notes: The census under Quirinius (Luke 2:2) and its dating relative to Herod's death is a known historical problem; the script says only that historians debate how it fits the records.
Augustus hailed as savior and bringer of peace in inscriptions (e.g. the Priene calendar inscription). Confirm.

Kataluma as guest room (Luke 22:11 'guestchamber') and the reading of a full family house with animals inside: a widely held scholarly view (e.g. Kenneth Bailey), not universal. Presented as 'many scholars think'.
The tomb hint (Luke 23:53; Joseph of Arimathea's tomb) is offered as what 'some see'.
